classification.name: ElaborateDrops
evidence: use crate::elaborate_drop::{DropElaborator, DropFlagMode, DropStyle, Unwind, elaborate_drop};
Fixes ICE, when type is provided in AsyncDrop trait instead of `async fn drop()`.

The changed code is the async-drop path of the drop-elaboration helper in elaborate_drop.rs. It is consumed by the registered `ElaborateDrops` MIR pass implemented in elaborate_drops.rs, which imports and calls that helper. The patch validates the AsyncDrop trait's candidate item before constructing the async drop call, converting an ICE into normal diagnostics; this is pass-specific drop-elaboration correctness knowledge.

analysis.originalLogic: In the async-drop branch of the drop-elaboration helper, the pass obtained the trait's drop function by taking the first associated item of the AsyncDrop trait unconditionally: `let Some(drop_fn_def_id) = tcx.associated_item_def_ids(drop_trait).into_iter().nth(0).copied()`. The surrounding comment says `impl_item_refs may be empty if drop fn is not implemented in 'impl AsyncDrop for ...'` and `Such code will report error, so just generate sync drop here and return`. The chosen def id was then assumed to be the async drop function when constructing the async drop call.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The pass treated the first associated item def id of the AsyncDrop trait as the drop function without validating either its definition kind or its signature. For malformed impls, that first item can be an associated type (`type c;` / `type c = ();`) or an associated function with an incompatible signature (`fn c(d: impl Sized) {}` or `fn drop(_wrong: impl Sized) {}`). Using such a def id as the drop function caused an ICE rather than normal diagnostics. The corrected transformation replaces the unconditional selection with a check that `tcx.def_kind(def_id) == DefKind::AssocFn && tcx.check_args_compatible(*def_id, trait_args)`, so an invalid candidate yields None and the existing fallback (`span_delayed_bug` plus generating a sync drop) is taken. This is a confirmed bug fix, not an optimization: the PR states it `Fixes ICE, when type is provided in AsyncDrop trait instead of async fn drop()` and `Fixes ICE, when async drop fn has wrong signature.`
analysis.inputDomain: Rust source using `#![feature(async_drop)]` (edition 2024) with an `impl AsyncDrop for T` whose associated item named/positioned as the drop function is either an associated type instead of the drop method, or is an associated function whose arguments/self type are incompatible with the trait's `async fn drop(self: Pin<&mut Self>)`. A value of `T` must be dropped in an async context so that async drop elaboration runs.
analysis.summary: ElaborateDrops' async-drop lookup blindly took the first associated item of the AsyncDrop trait as the drop function. It must instead require `DefKind::AssocFn` and `check_args_compatible` before constructing the async drop call; otherwise malformed impls (associated type instead of `drop`, or a `drop` with the wrong signature) trigger an ICE instead of normal diagnostics.
analysis.trigger: An `impl AsyncDrop for T` provides an associated type in place of the async drop function, or provides an associated function with an incompatible signature, and a `T` value is dropped inside an async function, causing drop elaboration to select that non-drop associated item and construct an async drop call from it.
preconditions: The crate enables `#![feature(async_drop)]` (tests use edition 2024 and incomplete-features allowance).

There is an `impl AsyncDrop for T` with a malformed associated item: either an associated type (`type c;`, `type c = ();`) instead of `drop`, or a method named/positioned as drop with an incompatible signature such as `fn c(d: impl Sized) {}` or `fn drop(_wrong: impl Sized) {}`.
A value of `T` is dropped in an async context (`async fn bar() { A; }`) so the ElaborateDrops pass elaborates the async drop.
The associated item at the inspected position is not guaranteed to be the drop function; selection must validate both `DefKind::AssocFn` and argument compatibility.
pitfalls: Taking the first element of `associated_item_def_ids(drop_trait)` does not guarantee that element is the drop function; associated types and other items can appear.
Checking only `DefKind::AssocFn` is insufficient: an associated function can still have an incompatible signature, so `check_args_compatible(*def_id, trait_args)` is also required.

When validation fails, the pass must fall through to the existing sync-drop fallback/diagnostic path instead of constructing an async drop call or emitting a delayed bug for valid-but-malformed user code.
The bug manifests specifically as an ICE on invalid programs; valid async drop implementations must still take the async drop path, so a fix that rejects all candidates would be wrong.
The regression tests were moved from `tests/crashes/` to `tests/ui/async-await/async-drop/`, so their expectations now include normal compiler diagnostics rather than known-bug crash markers.
analysis.testStrategy: Build two UI programs that differ only in the malformed AsyncDrop associated item (and a companion valid impl): (1) `impl AsyncDrop for a { type c = (); }` with `impl Drop for a { fn b() {} }`, expecting E0407/E0437/E0046 diagnostics without a crash (from #140484 / `unexpected-sort.rs`); (2) `impl AsyncDrop for A { fn drop(_wrong: impl Sized) {} }` with a valid `impl Drop for A { fn drop(&mut self) {} }`, expecting E0186 for the missing `self: Pin<&mut Self>` (from #140500 / `type-parameter.rs`). Include a value drop in `async fn bar() { A; }`. Use edition 2024, `#![feature(async_drop)]`, `#![crate_type = "lib"]`, and an incomplete-features allowance. Assert the emitted stderr matches the expected diagnostics and that no ICE/delayed-bug output occurs; also keep a control case with a valid `async fn drop` to confirm the async-drop path still elaborates. No execution was performed here, so these are source-based regression-test designs.
